beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new; this is the module title

beats.trigger: You can't really share an agent.
beats.got: I can't just hand my team my setup. That is exactly what I was about to try.

beats.trigger: Walk in with one example where people had access to a tool or process but real use did not follow.
beats.got: I'd already been thinking of our CRM rollout as that example.

beats.trigger: **Name** the likely adoption failure before it happens, including the social failure that's hardest to see
beats.got: nothing new; it's a list of five verbs. The failure-before-it-happens one is the only item I care about.

beats.trigger: who's the one person who came to mind just now? And what makes you hesitate about actually handing this to them?
beats.got: The person who came to mind is my pricing analyst. My hesitation is that he'd get a generic answer and quietly drop it.

beats.trigger: Your teammate doesn't want your agent. They want a job done.
beats.got: Start from the teammate's job, not from my tool. Sensible, but I already half knew it.

beats.trigger: does it name one teammate, their current way of doing the job, and an outcome you could observe?
beats.got: There is a concrete test for whether jtbd.md is good: one person, their current way of working, an observable outcome. I can use that to check output.

beats.trigger: If the reason is merely *"we already have the platform,"* send it back.
beats.got: I choose the sharing shape by the outcome, not by what tooling we have. That is a useful filter.

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: nothing new; it's a bridge to the next exercise

beats.trigger: Now find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can actually absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: The next 23 minutes are about the obstacle and a plan with two halves.

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: I look for the one obstacle that causes the others, not the first technical limit I notice. That is how I'd look at a pricing problem too.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: A people plan full of blanks is a result in itself. My team's plan would look exactly like that.

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact to `module-7/monday.md`
beats.got: nothing new; it's a bridge

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: The plans are hypotheses and we test them.

beats.trigger: *what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?*
beats.got: I turn adoption into a list of testable conditions. This is how I'd put it to my CFO.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: A pre-mortem that ends in one named person, one question and one test for next week. That is what I came for.

beats.trigger: Test the switch, not the solution.
beats.got: Four-line recap. It is tidy, but it repeats what I just did.

beats.trigger: The rest of this is about the person on the other end of your plan.
beats.got: nothing new; the lecture is about the recipient

beats.trigger: The outcome sentence is the contract: minimize or increase something, while doing that job.
beats.got: nothing new; this is the first beat again. The third outcome besides speed and quality is a small new point.

beats.trigger: Hand someone the agent file and they run it, get a generic answer, and quietly stop.
beats.got: The value sits in the curated memory and my corrections, not in the instructions file. So my prompts are not what I should be handing over.

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: Context, boundary and checks copy easily. Someone answering for the result does not copy.

beats.trigger: The two get reported as one number and they are not one thing.
beats.got: nothing new; this is the big idea again. The point about reporting access and absorption as one number is fair, but I've heard it.

beats.trigger: Michael Polanyi, a philosopher of science, had the line for it: *we know more than we can tell.*
beats.got: nothing I can use on Monday. This beat is philosophy and my attention is slipping.

beats.trigger: The interface is the first piece whose shape depends on somebody whose calendar you do not control.
beats.got: nothing new; I don't see why this is its own beat

beats.trigger: The leadership had not done the analysis. People they trusted had.
beats.got: A good analysis can stall because the deciders didn't do it themselves. That is a risk for my pricing proposal with the CFO and CEO.

beats.trigger: Not *how do I get them to adopt this?* but *what would have to be true for them to switch?*
beats.got: nothing new; I did this question in the exercise. The 'somebody they trust has to have used it first' example is the one useful detail.

beats.trigger: Whether they pick it up is their decision, made for their own reasons, on a Tuesday you will not be in the room for.
beats.got: nothing new; I can't force adoption

beats.trigger: So the move stays small. One name. One person whose week this would change, who would tell you plainly if it did not.
beats.got: Start with one person who will be honest with me. My analyst fits.

beats.trigger: The agent reviews, rewrites the sharing artifact in place, and reports what changed.
beats.got: Five minutes of the agent sharpening the artifact in place. Fine, but not exciting.

beats.trigger: The artifact: the sharpened sharing file itself, plus one line in your Module 7 next-step file naming the first move.
beats.got: nothing new; correct the summary and write one line for Monday

beats.trigger: Access is easy; absorption is scarce.
beats.got: nothing new; the recap repeats the big idea a third time

beats.trigger: Come to Module 8 without one tested assumption or named person and you'll be reconstructing the contact while the opening exercise is already using the evidence.
beats.got: I have homework before Module 8: run monday.md and bring back real evidence.

beats.trigger: What comes back from that contact is Module 8's raw material.
beats.got: nothing new

take_homes: Start from my analyst's actual job and the outcome he wants moved, and only then decide what to share. I don't hand over my setup.
Share the context (sources, my corrections, the style file) before sharing any prompt or agent file. That is why my team needs a shared home for the context files.
A blank in the people plan, such as who owns it or who answers for it, is a finding. Name one person and test one assumption before building more.

monday.move: Sit down with my pricing analyst and ask how he builds the pilot-cohort brief today. Then test one assumption from assumptions.md: whether he would use the brief if it landed in the place he already looks.
monday.who: The pricing analyst on my team, who will tell me plainly if it doesn't help.
monday.when: Monday morning, 30 minutes, before the pricing working group.
monday.stop_condition: If he says his current spreadsheet and gut call already do the job and I can't name what would change that, I stop building and write down why.
monday.blocker: There is still no shared place for the context files, so he would start from his own copy. I would have to pick that place first.

misconception.why: I came believing that getting good meant writing better prompts. The module says the value sits in curated context, corrections and judgement, and that the instructions file alone gives a generic answer. I wouldn't say I've changed my mind, because I haven't tried it on my own team yet.

one_line: The exercises are good and gave me a real Monday move. The lecture repeats the big idea three times, but the value-stream story and the people-plan-stalls-on-names point are worth the hour.
